title: Order and effort
hook: all is within the hukam, yet the Gurus ask us to strive

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Nanak's aarti: the sky as the tray, and the light in everything. Your line was beyond and within. At dusk, what did you see in the sky, and in the person near you? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-six.

A farmer in Punjab can't make it rain. She can't choose the heat, or the day the monsoon arrives, or whether a storm flattens the wheat a week before harvest. All of that is out of her hands. And still, every season, she's up before light: plowing, sowing, watering, mending the channel where the water runs. Nobody would call her lazy for not controlling the sky, and nobody would call her wise for sitting in the doorway waiting for it. She works inside something larger than her work. Today's idea is that farmer's life, put as a question Sikh thought takes seriously: if everything happens within God's order, why try?
screen: `SHE CAN'T MAKE IT RAIN.` → `UP BEFORE LIGHT, EVERY SEASON.` → `IF ALL IS ORDERED, WHY TRY?`

segments.voice: Start with the order. Hukam is the Granth's word for it: the command, the will, the way the One runs everything. In the second pauri of Japji, Guru Nanak says it in paraphrase: by hukam all forms are made; by hukam some are high and some low, some get joy and some get pain. And then the line that leaves no gaps: everyone is within the hukam, and no one is outside it. And yet the same scripture is full of work. Guru Arjan, in a short verse, says in paraphrase: make the effort, and earning by it, live in peace; meditating, you meet the Lord. Sikh life is built on this. Kirat karo, earn an honest living, is one of the pillars Sikhs name alongside remembering the Name and sharing. How do the two fit? Sikh teachers say hukam is not fate in the sense of a script you sit and watch. It's closer to the farmer's sky: the frame you live inside. Your effort is part of the order, not a fight against it. Japji's answer to the question of how to live is, in paraphrase, to walk in the way of the hukam, the will. Walking is still walking. You still lift your feet. That takes a weight off. If everything depended on your effort alone, every failure would be total. If nothing did, there'd be no reason to get up. Within the order, you do your part fully, and then let the rest be what it is. Strive within the order.
screen: `HUKAM: NO ONE IS OUTSIDE IT.` · `MAKE THE EFFORT, LIVE IN PEACE.` · `NOT A SCRIPT, A SKY TO WORK UNDER.` · `DO YOUR PART; LET THE REST BE.` · then, large: `STRIVE WITHIN THE ORDER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do your part today. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing that's worrying you. Gently split it in two. On one side, the part that's yours: a call you could make, a task you could start, an apology you could offer. On the other side, the part that isn't: other people's choices, the weather, the outcome. Choose one small piece from your side and decide when you'll do it. Then, with each out-breath, set the other side down. The bell holds the time.
Order and effort. Everything is within the hukam, and still the Gurus ask for honest work and striving: your effort is part of the order. Today's word.
Your line: strive within the order. Today, do the one small piece that's yours, fully, and when it's done, let the result go. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite Japji Sahib, which says all are within the hukam, each morning, and they hold honest work, kirat karo, alongside remembering the Name and sharing as part of daily Sikh life.

fork.setup: you're a farmer, and you can't control the rain. the season is starting. what do you do?
options: sit in the doorway; it's all in God's hands anyway.
plow and sow, and leave the sky to the order.
refuse to plant until the weather is certain.
fork.reveal: the Gurus ask for striving within the hukam: do your part fully, and let the rest be.

original.note: Gurmukhi: command, will, order: the way the One runs everything.

trapdoor: what you thought: hukam means fate, so nothing you do matters.
what it means: the order everyone lives within, and your effort is part of it.
what a scholar hears: Japji's second pauri says no one is outside the hukam, and its first answers how to live: walk in the way of the will.

sources.ref: Ang 522 (Gujri ki Var, slok, Guru Arjan)

notes: Paraphrase of Japji pauri 2 ('hukmee hovan aakaar... hukmai andar sabh ko, baahar hukam na koe') and pauri 1 ('hukam rajaaee chalnaa'); please confirm.
Paraphrase of 'udam karediaa jeeo toon kamavdiaa sukh bhunch, dhiaaidiaa toon prabhoo mil' attributed to Guru Arjan at Ang 522; please confirm the Ang and wording.
Kirat karo named alongside naam japo and vand chhako as 'pillars Sikhs name'; please confirm the framing.
The Punjab farmer in the hook is an illustrative scene, not a sourced story.
